u1s2: A spring is a natural exit point at which groundwater emerges from an aquifer and flows across the ground surface as surface water.
u2s2: Springs have long been important for humans as a source of fresh water, especially in arid regions which have relatively little annual rainfall.
u3s2: A spring produced by the emergence of geothermally heated groundwater is known as a hot spring.
u4s2: The yield of spring water varies widely from a volumetric flow rate of nearly zero to more than 14,000 litres per second (490 cu ft/s) for the biggest springs.
u5s2: Springs may also be formed as a result of karst topography, aquifers or volcanic activity.
u6s2: Springs have also been observed on the ocean floor, spewing warmer, low-salinity water directly into the ocean.
u7s2: Springs formed as a result of karst topography create karst springs, in which ground water travels through a network of cracks and fissures—openings ranging from intergranular spaces to large caves, later emerging in a spring.
u8s2: The forcing of the spring to the surface can be the result of a confined aquifer in which the recharge area of the spring water table rests at a higher elevation than that of the outlet.
u9s2: Spring water forced to the surface by elevated sources are artesian wells.
u10s2: Non-artesian springs may simply flow from a higher elevation through the earth to a lower elevation and exit in the form of a spring, using the ground like a drainage pipe.
u11s2: Still other springs are the result of pressure from an underground source in the earth, in the form of volcanic or magma activity.
u12s2: The result can be water at elevated temperature and pressure, i.e. hot springs and geysers.
u13s2: === Types === Depression springs occur along a depression, such as the bottom of alluvial valleys, basins, or valleys made of highly permeable materials.
u14s2: Contact springs, which occur along the side of a hill or mountain, are created when the groundwater is underlaid by an impermeable layer of rock or soil known as an aquiclude or aquifuge Fracture, or joint occur when groundwater running along an impermeable layer of rock meets a crack (fracture) or joint in the rock.
u15s2: Tubular springs occur when groundwater flows from circular fissures such as those found in caverns (solution tubular springs) or lava tubular springs found in lava tube caves.
u16s2: Artesian springs typically occur at the lowest point in a given area.
u17s2: An artesian spring is created when the pressure for the groundwater becomes greater than the pressure from the atmosphere.
u18s2: Karst springs occur as outflows of groundwater that are part of a karst hydrological system.
u19s2: Thermal springs are heated by geothermal activity; they have a water temperature significantly higher than the mean air temperature of the surrounding area.
u20s2: Geysers are a type of hot spring where steam is created underground by trapped superheated groundwater resulting in recurring eruptions of hot water and steam.
u21s2: Carbonated springs, such as Soda Springs Geyser, are springs that emit naturally occurring carbonated water, due to dissolved carbon dioxide in the water content.
u22s2: They are sometimes called boiling springs or bubbling springs.
u23s2: "Gushette springs pour from cliff faces" Helocrene springs are diffuse that sustain marshlands with groundwater.
u24s2: == Flow == Spring discharge, or resurgence, is determined by the spring's recharge basin.
u25s2: Factors that affect the recharge include the size of the area in which groundwater is captured, the amount of precipitation, the size of capture points, and the size of the spring outlet.
u26s2: Human activity may also affect a spring's discharge—withdrawal of groundwater reduces the water pressure in an aquifer, decreasing the volume of flow.
u27s2: === Classification === Springs fall into three general classifications: perennial (springs that flow constantly during the year); intermittent (temporary springs that are active after rainfall, or during certain seasonal changes); and periodic (as in geysers that vent and erupt at regular or irregular intervals).
u28s2: Springs are often classified by the volume of the water they discharge.
u29s2: The largest springs are called "first-magnitude", defined as springs that discharge water at a rate of at least 2800 liters or 100 cubic feet (2.8 m3) of water per second.
u30s2: Some locations contain many first-magnitude springs, such as Florida where there are at least 27 known to be that size; the Missouri and Arkansas Ozarks, which contain 10 known of first-magnitude; and 11 more in the Thousand Springs area along the Snake River in Idaho.
u31s2: The scale for spring flow is as follows: == Water content == Minerals become dissolved in the water as it moves through the underground rocks.
u32s2: This is why spring water is often bottled and sold as mineral water, although the term is often the subject of deceptive advertising.
u33s2: Springs that contain significant amounts of minerals are sometimes called 'mineral springs'.
u34s2: (Springs without such mineral content, meanwhile, are sometimes distinguished as 'sweet springs'.)
u35s2: Springs that contain large amounts of dissolved sodium salts, mostly sodium carbonate, are called 'soda springs'.
u36s2: Many resorts have developed around mineral springs and are known as spa towns.
u37s2: Mineral springs are alleged to have healing properties.
u38s2: Some springs contain arsenic levels that exceed the 10 ppb World Health Organization (WHO) standard for drinking water.
u39s2: Where such springs feed rivers they can also raise the arsenic levels in the rivers above WHO limits.
u40s2: Water from springs is usually clear.
u41s2: However, some springs may be coloured by the minerals that are dissolved in the water.
u42s2: In parts of the United States a stream carrying the outflow of a spring to a nearby primary stream may be called a spring branch, spring creek, or run.
u43s2: Groundwater tends to maintain a relatively long-term average temperature of its aquifer; so flow from a spring may be cooler than other sources on a summer day, but remain unfrozen in the winter.
u44s2: The cool water of a spring and its branch may harbor species such as certain trout that are otherwise ill-suited to a warmer local climate.
u45s2: === Types of mineral springs === Sulfur springs contain a high level of dissolved sulfur or hydrogen sulfide in the water.
u46s2: Borax springs Gypsum springs Saline springs Iron springs (chalybeate spring) Radium springs (or radioactive springs) have a detectable level of radiation produced by the natural radioactive decay process == Uses == Springs have been used for a variety of human needs - including drinking water, domestic water supply, irrigation, mills, navigation, and electricity generation.
u47s2: Modern uses include recreational activities such as fishing, swimming, and floating; therapy; water for livestock; fish hatcheries; and supply for bottled mineral water or bottled spring water.
u48s2: Springs have taken on a kind of mythic quality in that some people falsely believe that springs are always healthy sources of drinking water.
u49s2: One must take a comprehensive water quality test to know how to use a spring appropriately, whether for a mineral bath or drinking water.
u50s2: Springs that are managed as spas will already have such a test.
u51s2: When purchasing bottled water labeled as spring water one can often find the water test for that spring on the website of the company selling it.
u52s2: Indigenous people of the American Southwest built spring-fed acequias that directed water to fields through canals.
u53s2: === Sacred springs === A sacred spring, or holy well, is a small body of water emerging from underground and revered in some religious context: Christian and/or pagan and/or other.
u54s2: The lore and mythology of ancient Greece was replete with sacred and storied springs—notably, the Corycian, Pierian and Castalian springs.
u55s2: The term "holy well" is commonly employed to refer to any water source of limited size (i.e., not a lake or river, but including pools and natural springs and seeps), which has some significance in local folklore.
u56s2: Christian legends often recount how the action of a saint caused a spring's water to flow - a familiar theme, especially in the hagiography of Celtic saints.
u57s2: === Thermal springs === The geothermally heated groundwater that flows from thermal springs is greater than human body temperature, usually in the range of 45–50 °C (113–122 °F), but they can be hotter.
u58s2: Those springs with water cooler than body temperature but warmer than air temperature are sometimes referred to as warm springs.
u59s2: ==== Bathing and balneotherapy ==== Hot springs or geothermal springs have been used for balneotherapy, bathing, and relaxation for thousands of years.
u60s2: Because of the folklore surrounding hot springs and their claimed medical value, some have become tourist destinations and locations of physical rehabilitation centers.
u61s2: ==== Geothermal energy ==== Hot springs have been used as a heat source for thousands of years.
u62s2: The city of Beppu, Japan contains 2,217 hot spring well heads that provide the city with hot water.
u63s2: Hot springs have also been used as a source of sustainable energy for greenhouse cultivation and the growing of crops and flowers.
u64s2: == Terminology == Spring boil Spring pool Spring runs also called rheocrene springs Spring vent == Cultural representations == Springs have been represented in culture through art, mythology, and folklore throughout history.
u65s2: The Fountain of Youth is a mythical spring which was said to restore youth to anyone who drank from it.
u66s2: It is believed that the vapors were emitted from the Kerna spring at Delphi.
u67s2: The Greek myth of Narcissus describes a young man who fell in love with his reflection in the still pool of a spring.
u68s2: Narcissus gazed into "an unmuddied spring, silvery from its glittering waters, which neither shepherds nor she-goats grazing on the mountain nor any other cattle had touched, which neither bird nor beast nor branch fallen from a tree had disturbed."
u69s2: (Ovid) The early 20th century American photographer, James Reuel Smith created a comprehensive series of photographs documenting the historical springs of New York City before they were capped by the city after the advent of the municipal water system.
u70s2: Smith later photographed springs in Europe leading to his book, Springs and Wells in Greek and Roman Literature, Their Legends and Locations (1922).
u71s2: The Chinese city Jinan is known as "a City of Springs" (Chinese: 泉城), because of its 72 spring attractions and numerous micro spring holes spread over the city centre.
